title: Can PBR's 280,000-BPD Capacity Expansion Drive Cash Flow Growth? - The Globe and Mail
content: Brazil's state-run energy giant Petroleo Brasileiro S.A., or Petrobras (PBR), is increasing oil production by improving the efficiency of its existing offshore platforms. In its latest earnings call, management stated that 11 platforms have received authorization to operate above their original design capacity. These platforms now have approximately 280,000 barrels per day of additional production capacity. Petrobras achieved this increase without spending on new production platforms, although additional wells and subsea equipment are needed to use the available capacity. The initiative allows the company to increase production while limiting spending on new infrastructure. The improvements are already contributing to Petrobras' output. Through October 2026, the 11 platforms generated average incremental production of approximately 90,000 barrels per day. Petrobras has identified six more platforms for similar capacity increases, targeting another 260,000 barrels per day. Together, these initiatives offer the potential to add more than 500,000 barrels per day of production capacity. Management is working to connect additional wells and improve reservoir performance to make greater use of this capacity. The pace of these activities will determine how quickly the company can increase actual production. Building new offshore production facilities requires significant investment and several years before production begins. By increasing output from operating platforms, Petrobras can bring additional barrels to market sooner and avoid some spending associated with new facilities. Higher production from existing assets can support cash generation and improve capital efficiency, especially when oil prices remain favorable. However, the financial benefits will depend on how much additional production Petrobras achieves, the costs of connecting new wells and changes in crude prices. Petrobras’ offshore expansion highlights a broader challenge for oil producers: how to grow output while keeping development costs in check. U.S. energy majors ChevronCVX and ExxonMobil HoldingsXOM face the same trade-off, with Chevron expanding capacity at existing facilities and ExxonMobil looking to improve drilling productivity. Chevron is increasing production by expanding capacity at existing facilities through capital-efficient debottlenecking projects. In its latest earnings call, management said these projects have added more than 85,000 barrels per day of upstream capacity. Chevron has also increased processing capacity at Tengiz by 20% and facility capacity at Anchor by 33%. These improvements can support production growth while limiting investment in new infrastructure. Meanwhile, ExxonMobil is also focusing on improving operational efficiency to increase production and lower costs. In the Permian Basin, ExxonMobil is deploying automated drilling rigs to improve drilling performance and productivity. The company currently operates three such rigs and plans to expand their use to approximately 25% of its Permian fleet in 2027 and 50% by 2028. These improvements can help ExxonMobil increase production while managing development costs. Shares of PBR have gained around 27.6% over the past year, slightly underperforming the industry’s growth. Petrobras currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.61 on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by nine brokerage firms. title: Chevron’s 39% Gain Rests On A Supply Squeeze - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? Over the past twelve months, Chevron (CVX) stock returned 39.3%, compared with 9.7% for the S&P 500. Profits also climbed over the past year, and the share price rests on those profits. Yet part of that profit comes from markets management describes as tight for now. So what is lifting Chevron’s profits right now, and how long can it last? Chevron Is Earning More While Conflicts Squeeze Supply Chevron has been selling into a global fuel shortage. On its October 30, 2026 call, management said the world has 10% of its refining capacity offline, with exports reduced due to the conflicts. Prices have also swung widely. Management said they ran from $68 to $132 a barrel in fiscal Q3 2026 alone. Chevron sold into prices that swung from $68 to $132 a barrel in a single quarter. If Chevron makes up a big piece of your savings, you feel every one of those swings. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record. Management does not expect this to last for good. It expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term. In chemicals, it was more cautious about the longer run. Once flows normalize, markets may very well return to oversupply, unless some capacity closes or projects are deferred. Chevron has seen a peak like this before. Its operating margin was 14.6% over the twelve months to September 2026, compared with 8.1% a year earlier. The last September it stood higher was 2022, at 16.2%. Measured each September, the margin then fell in each of the next three years, back to 8.1% by 2025. Chevron’s downstream business, which holds its refineries, brought in $142 billion in fiscal 2025. That is more revenue than its upstream business brought in, at $88.4 billion. Downstream revenue fell 9.8% from fiscal 2024, so its sales were already falling before 2026. Then Chevron’s total revenue, across all its businesses, jumped. After growing just 3.2% from a year earlier in fiscal Q1 2026, it rose 51.4% in fiscal Q2. Growth was still 35.4% in fiscal Q3. Some of the gain is Chevron’s own work. Management said its refineries reached record quarterly U.S. crude throughput, helped by added capacity at refineries such as Pasadena. That capacity stays with Chevron whatever happens to the shortage. Chevron stock closed 11.6% below its one-year high on November 19, 2026. It trades at 15.0 times its past year’s earnings, compared with 21.5 for the S&P 500. The price appears to assume that some of today’s profit will not last. Chevron fell further than the S&P 500 in three of the four recent market shocks in our data. In the 2024 yen carry trade unwind, it fell 8.2% against 7.8%. In the 2023 yield shock, it fell 12.0% compared with 9.5% for the index, and in the 2023 regional banking crisis, it fell 10.0% against 6.7%. The 2025 tariff shock was an exception, with Chevron down 15.0% against 19.0%. The bigger risk is that the supply squeeze ends and takes the extra profit with it. Management expects chemical margins to stay a bit elevated at least through the end of 2026, maybe into 2027. For the risk to be worth taking, Chevron’s own growth would need to hold profits up once supply returns. That includes its plan to double output from its Venezuela ventures to roughly 600,000 barrels a day by 2031. Chevron is expected to report its fourth-quarter results in January 2027. That report will show how its downstream earnings moved from the third quarter. After a year like this one, Chevron may now be a bigger share of your savings than you planned. It is worth deciding how you would step back from it while the gain is still there. If Chevron is a big part of your wealth, so are its risk and its tax bill. What’s your exit plan? Chevron occupies a distinctive spot in the energy world, pairing enormous scale with a freshly deepened pool of advantaged assets after the Hess deal. With the calendar turning toward year-end, the near-term focus shifts to execution. The pace of the Hess integration, Permian well productivity and the cadence of Guyana startups will shape how the current quarter unfolds, and the company's long record of managing complex projects is one reason the name is watched so closely at this point in the cycle. No producer is immune to the crosscurrents of the moment. Integrated majors must navigate soft crude prices, swinging refining margins and the long-run pressure to lower the carbon intensity of their operations. What sets the company apart is the breadth of its model and, after the Hess deal, its enlarged stake in the prized Guyana play, a combination that gives it a distinct position in a market where most rivals specialize in one slice of the chain. Because of its size and visibility, Chevron functions as a barometer for the health of the global oil and gas business and the broader energy complex. Earnings rose sharply compared with last year, while cash generation remained robust. For readers who follow Oil and Gas Stocks, Chevron is a key industry benchmark known for its dividend and capital discipline. The company is a large member of the Russell 1000, and its results shape sentiment across the energy sector. Reported earnings nearly tripled from the same quarter last year, and adjusted earnings grew even faster. Total revenues rose at a strong double-digit pace. Compared with the second quarter, however, adjusted earnings declined. Return on capital employed was solid, and the company generated strong adjusted free cash flow, supported by a loan repayment from its Kazakhstan joint venture and proceeds from asset sales. Downstream earnings in the United States rose dramatically from a year earlier. Wider margins on refined products, especially diesel, were the main driver. Chevron's US refineries processed record amounts of crude oil and operated at very high utilization. Its Pascagoula refinery achieved a multi-year diesel production record, and US distillate yield was strong. Global fuel markets have been tight, partly because wars in the Middle East and Ukraine disrupted supply. When refined fuels like diesel and jet fuel are scarce, refiners earn larger margins. Chevron benefited from running its plants reliably during this period. US upstream earnings rose strongly from a year earlier, helped by higher oil prices and lower operating costs. US production exceeded two million barrels of oil equivalent per day for the fifth straight quarter, and the Permian Basin maintained high output. Chevron also set records for natural gas production, led by Australia and the Eastern Mediterranean, and for deepwater output in the Gulf. International production fell compared with a year earlier. Higher oil prices reduced Chevron's entitlement volumes under certain contracts, and conflict in the Middle East disrupted some operations. These declines were partly offset by record Australian output, higher Gulf production and the inclusion of one month of Venezuelan production following an accounting change. Chevron expanded its acreage in Venezuela, where it is making a large investment. In the Bakken region, it expects a restructuring of midstream contracts to sharply reduce transportation tariffs, improve returns and add flexibility. This transaction will require a one-time non-cash accounting loss when it closes. Integration of last year's large acquisition continues to support production and cost savings. Organic capital spending was lower than a year earlier, largely due to reduced Permian investment. Management expects fourth-quarter spending to rise but still finish the year at the low end of its annual range. Disciplined spending supports free cash flow and returns to investors. Chevron has a long history of dividend increases and regular share repurchases. Strong free cash flow, especially during periods of high margins, allows the company to fund both. Its integrated model, combining production and refining, helps stabilize cash generation across different price environments. Chevron is applying digital tools and advanced data analysis to improve drilling efficiency, refinery reliability and exploration success. In the Permian Basin, better well designs and longer laterals have helped maintain high output with lower capital spending. These efficiency gains support the company's goal of growing free cash flow without large increases in investment. Chevron's partnership in the Tengiz field in Kazakhstan is one of its largest sources of oil. A recent expansion project has brought operations close to full rates, increasing cash distributions to Chevron. The joint venture also repaid a loan to Chevron during the quarter, boosting free cash flow. Risks include falling oil prices, a return to normal refining margins, geopolitical disruptions, political risks in Venezuela and Kazakhstan, the accounting loss from the Bakken restructuring and project execution challenges. Energy transition policies may also affect long-term demand. Chevron and other large integrated oil companies both benefited from strong refining margins this quarter. Chevron's record US refinery throughput, natural gas records and disciplined spending stood out. Its Kazakhstan operations and Venezuela expansion give it unique growth exposures compared with peers. Chevron nearly tripled its earnings on record US refinery throughput and strong fuel margins, while generating substantial free cash flow. Production records in key areas offset some international disruptions, and geopolitical developments remain the main factor to watch. title: Your Chevron Hedge Works Only While Oil Spikes - Trefis
content: Our Nov 18 look at Chevron found the stock moving on its own. Chevron gained 2.3% from November 10 to November 17, while the S&P 500 lost 2.4%. For the full record, see Is Chevron Stock Increasing Your Market Risk? The next question is whether Chevron protects a portfolio when oil prices jump. The short answer is yes during the spike month, and usually no in the months after it. In the month of a spike, Chevron beat the market in 19 of 26 cases. Over the three months after a spike, it beat the market in only 9 of 25 cases. In an ordinary three-month stretch, it beats the market 48.6% of the time. The common view is that energy stocks jump when oil supply looks tight. The data agrees for the spike month itself. This piece looks at what came after. We set a rule in advance. A spike month is a calendar month in which USO, a fund built to follow oil prices, rose 10% or more. Since 2006, that happened in 26 months. Those months form 21 separate episodes. We compared Chevron with SPY, a fund that tracks the S&P 500. In the spike month, Chevron averaged a 7.7% gain. SPY averaged 2.1%. October 2026 was one of those months. USO rose 15.9%. Chevron rose 15.3%, while SPY slipped 0.91%. Since then, the move has reversed. From the Oct 30 close to Wednesday’s close, USO fell 19.4%. Chevron returned -11.9%, against -3.4% for SPY. Chevron has given back 11.9% since the end of October. If you own it mainly for its income, you may want income that does not rise and fall with the price of oil. Meanwhile, the Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500’s, from 50 stocks with at least 10 straight years of dividends. See what it pays. Chevron closed at $205.88 on Wednesday, Nov 18. That was 4.7% below Tuesday’s close of $216.13. Part of the drop was the dividend. Wednesday was the ex-dividend date, the first day a buyer no longer gets the next payout. Counting the dividend, Chevron returned -4.0%. Other energy names and oil itself fell with it on Wednesday: Our data does not show why these stocks fell on Wednesday. Not usually. In the month after a spike, Chevron beat SPY in 11 of 25 cases, or 44%. In an ordinary one-month stretch, it beats SPY 49.4% of the time. Its median return that next month was -0.63%, against 1.3% for SPY. Over three months, the gap widens. Chevron beat SPY in 9 of 25 cases, or 36%. Its median three-month return was 0.40%, against 4.1% for SPY. October 2026 is left out of these counts because its windows are not complete. The table below shows how often each of three energy stocks beat SPY, in the spike month and after it. Source: Trefis analysis of Intrinio prices, May 2006 to October 2026. Prices are adjusted for splits and dividends. A spike month is a month when USO closed at least 10% above the prior month-end close. Chevron led the group in the spike month. It then had the weakest three-month record of the three. Think of a $1 million portfolio with 5% in Chevron and the rest in SPY. We compared it with a portfolio fully in SPY, held without changes. The Chevron slice changed the result this way: The range was wide. The best three-month case added $22,414. The worst cost $17,137. The record has clear exceptions. After December 2021, Chevron returned 40.2% over three months. SPY lost 4.6% over the same stretch. The opposite case is recent. March 2026 was the biggest USO month in the record, at 55.3%. Chevron rose 10.8% that month while SPY fell 4.9%. Over the next three months, Chevron lost about 19% while SPY gained 15.1%. Exxon Mobil held up better than Chevron over the three months after a spike. It beat SPY in 12 of 25 three-month windows. That is above its own normal rate of 42.4%. For a closer look at Exxon, see What Is Going On With Exxon Mobil Stock? The record shows a tendency, not a rule. We think a new oil spike could again lift Chevron during the spike itself. If history is a guide, it would not be a surprise if Chevron trailed the market over the following three months. December 2021 shows the pattern can break. The bigger question of how energy dividends compare with AI growth is in our piece Dividend Stocks Or AI Stocks: Which Fits Now? Our read: Chevron has protected a portfolio during an oil spike, not after it. Much of October’s gain is already gone. If Chevron grew into a large share of your money during that run, it helps to decide now when you would trim it. If Chevron is a big part of your wealth, so are its risk and its tax bill. title: Is Chevron Stock Increasing Your Market Risk? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036? Investors holding Chevron (CVX) alongside a broader index fund may have noticed the stock moving on its own. Chevron’s share price rose 1.5% from November 10 to November 17, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 2.4%. A stock that detaches from the index changes how a bad market day affects a portfolio. So when the market falls, does Chevron fall with the rest of your money? On average, no: in the year to November 17, 2026, Chevron tended to move the opposite way to the index. On the average day the S&P 500 fell, a drop of 0.632%, a $10,000 holding in Chevron gained about $58. On the average day the index rose by 0.667%, that same holding lost about $25. Beta measures how far a stock moves for each 1% the index moves. Chevron’s beta was -0.51 over that year. Across all days, the stock tended to move about half as far as the index, in the opposite direction. It fell on the index’s three worst days, though: on November 5, 2026, when the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, Chevron fell 1.9%. It also fell 0.6% on each of the index’s next two worst days. The index fell 2.6% on June 5, 2026, and 2.1% on January 20, 2026. Chevron also exhibited wider swings on its own. The stock’s volatility, a measure of how widely the price swings over a year, was 24.6% over the past year, against 13.8% for the index. Chevron therefore pulled some broader market risk out of a portfolio, but it introduced larger price swings of its own. Chevron’s swings are likely to stay wide, because its earnings move with oil and fuel prices that management calls very volatile. On the October 30, 2026 call, management said oil traded as low as $68 and as high as $132 a barrel within the third quarter. It said adjusted upstream earnings, from producing oil and gas, fell from the second quarter. The causes were lower realized prices, lower volumes sold and unfavorable timing effects. Adjusted downstream earnings rose on higher refining margins. Management also expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term, with 10% of the world’s refining capacity offline. Chevron’s pull against the market is less certain to last. Its correlation with the index, a score from -1 to 1 of how closely two prices move together, was -0.29 over the past year. That figure stood at 0.29 over the five years from November 2021, reflecting a loose tendency to move with the market rather than against it. Yes, by a little. Including dividends, Chevron returned 17.6% a year from November 9, 2021 to November 17, 2026. The S&P 500 returned 10.9% a year over the same dates. Its annual volatility over those five years was 25.4%, against 17.2% for the index. Chevron earned 0.693 of yearly return for each unit of swing, against 0.634 for the index. So Chevron’s swings have paid slightly better than the market’s. Management said Chevron has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years. Chevron tended to slip slightly on the market’s good days and gain on its bad ones over the past year. Held beside an index fund, the stock has on average offset part of the market’s moves in both directions. It still fell on the index’s three worst days of the year. For investors who already own oil producers, refiners or an energy fund, buying Chevron adds more of that same bet on oil and fuel prices. Chevron’s refining margins are the measure to watch at its next report, expected in January 2027. Chevron’s return over those five years included a dividend that management keeps raising.
